utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say good afternoon to the interpreters and to be sure that they hear me speaking, I hope they have had a good weekend. Then, of course, I would like to say good afternoon both to the Defence and to the Prosecution counsel, and to the accused, and to the Trial Chamber's legal officer. Now we can continue with the re-examination, which is part of the procedure pursuant to our Rules, which we can do as soon as Mr. Dundas-Whatley has come into the courtroom at request of the registrar. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, good afternoon, did you rest up a bit over the weekend? Do you feel good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's good. Mr. Hayman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Whatley, I will be jumping around to touch briefly on several different topics raised in your cross-examination at the end of last week. First, on cross-examination you were asked about the level of military experience of Lieutenant Colonel Watters and Lieutenant Colonel Thomas, also of the Cheshire Regiment and also witnesses who testified in this case. First, let me ask you a few questions about the service in Bosnia-Herzegovina of Lieutenant Colonel Brian Watters. As the second in command of the Cheshire Regiment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did his duties take him off of the British Battalion's base on a regular or daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on a daily basis, but occasionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How frequently he had contact with HVO and BH army commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but he did have contact with commanders, usually if there was a high level meeting taking place and Bob Stewart wasn't available, and perhaps Brian Watters would help chair that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that have been a regular or frequent occurrence, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly early on it was hardly ever, but I think towards the end, the last couple of weeks of our time there, it probably happened once or twice a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Lieutenant Colonel Watters serve with the regiment during its complete tour of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't. He came out to replace the second in command who had been there up until about the second week of February, '93, that's when Major Watters, as he was then, arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thus he would have arrived about midway through the tour of duty, is that right, and only been in Bosnia-Herzegovina the latter half?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant Colonel Thomas, he was a company commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he serve part of his service in Bosnia-Herzegovina in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. His company was posted to Tuzla for some time, and back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would his company, or the platoons in his company, have been principally involved in liaison work or other types of patrol or operative work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, his platoons and he, indeed, were not liaison officers, that was our job. He was a rifle platoon -- I'm sorry, rifle company commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thus, how frequently, if you know, did he have contacts with battalion or brigade commanders, either in the HVO or the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know for certain how often he had meetings with senior commanders. I think most of the contact that the company commanders had was with checkpoints, but I do know of one or two occasions where he did meet brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina for seven months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to summarise, you worked in the field an average of, you said about six days per week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many meetings per day, on average, would you have had with local commanders of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would, of course, vary. A normal day would probably be three meetings, and a busy day could be anything up to about ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you had four meetings a day on average, that would work out, I believe, to be 25 days or so per month, six months, four meetings per day, about 600 meetings with local commanders during your tour of duty; is that a fair, rough, very rough estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rough estimate, I think it is probably about right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you earlier today to count in your notes how many meetings, or documented in your notes with local commanders on the 15th of April, 1993. Have you counted that figure for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many meetings did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten that are documented in my notebook. Ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the 1st of March to the 16th of April, did anyone in the British Battalion have as many contacts as you did with the HVO and BH army commanders Vitez and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point in cross-examination you described using a BiH army radio to arrange a meeting with a Serb commander across the front-lines, I believe west of Travnik. Could you describe that experience for the Court? You weren't able to fully describe it during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I frequently went to the Bosnian army communications centre in Travnik, the purpose of which was to establish contact with the Serb army, the VRS. In order to do that, we, I would go into the communications room with Baba Salko, who I mentioned before, a very brave and honourable man, and we would, he would instruct the gentlemen operating the communications equipment to re-tune the radio into a Serb frequency. In the process of doing that, they would flick through frequencies and my interpreter would tell me which, listening to the conversations they were having, tell me which frequency or which organisations unit they are broken into. They would say, "Oh, that's the Bosnian army on the Vlasic, or that's the HVO in Novi Travnik, or that's the -- all right, we have got the Serbs now, that's good -- oh, no, it's the wrong Serb unit," so they would re-tune and go to another Serb unit. The point was that it became very obvious to us in December '92, that an enormous amount of military traffic between, or within the warring factions armies, was conducted over open VHF radios, and it was easy for the communication centre to re-tune through these frequencies. Then they would tune to a frequency that seemed appropriate for what we wanted to do, and the radio operator would start then calling on that frequency to interrupt the conversations taking place, and we would then establish communications with the Serbs that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time you arranged a meeting with the Serb commander, that is a meeting between a Serb commander and UNPROFOR representatives, was that before or after the 1st of March when you were assigned on a full-time basis to the Travnik Vitez, Novi Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was long before the 1st of March. My first across-the-front-line-meeting with the Serbs was in December, '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that meeting arranged in the way you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked on cross-examination, if you were a commander, would you have investigated the events in Ahmici? Who in the British army is responsible for investigating serious violations of military discipline, including criminal violations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The royal military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do they have specialised training in that function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, they are the police force of the British army, they are trained to investigate crimes, and they work to a very high level chain of command, they don't work for battalion or brigade commanders, they work at a much higher level; but that is their function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have said that command and control in the HVO was poor. If a commander's ability to command and control the military police was also poor, what would the effect be on that commander's ability to investigate serious violations of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would probably be totally impossible to investigate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military police, like any police force, is expected to be, to act in a thoroughly legal way, because they are the enforcers and the regulators of military discipline, particularly in relation to crimes and serious breaches of discipline. If the military police failed to conduct their business properly, and there is no other way, there is no other system that I'm aware of, certainly in the British system, that I'm aware of, other than them investigating themselves, other than the military police sorting out their own internal problems, that a breakdown of discipline of that nature can be dealt with. I think that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have given you copies of certain exhibits you were shown during your direct examination in order to save time. Do you have Exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 539 before you? That's the MILINFOSUM of the 8th of April, 1993. And if we could activate the ELMO so it can be used, please. I'll be directing your attention to paragraph 6, and I also have a copy. Why don't I give you a copy. I will place my copy on the ELMO for convenience. Have you had a chance to compare paragraph 6 of Exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 539 with the notes in your notebook from entries dated 8th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are there entries in paragraph 6, which is the paragraph titled "Travnik" and is now visible on the ELMO, are there entries which correspond to entries in your notes, including specific time references?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The paragraph begins "An LO team"; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that a reference to, what is an LO team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An LO team is a liaison officer, in this case me, plus my driver, my interpreter and the other members of my team, I would have an escort of some soldiers who would act as my personal protection, and possibly a second vehicle to support my vehicle, and that would all together be called an LO team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you the LO referred to as the LO team in paragraph 6 of Exhibit P539?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these MILINFOSUMs which were produced, did you write them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any decisions concerning what went in or what was omitted from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that someone else's job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the responsibility of the military information officer and his staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're done with that exhibit, you can put it aside. You were asked on cross-examination about alcohol consumption by the liaison officers. Why was it that the liaison officers of the British battalion were frequently served alcohol in the course of their working day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a bit of a custom that we found when we visited the headquarters of brigades and civilian organisations, as well. We would always be given a cup of coffee and a glass of plum brandy; so, depending how many meetings we went to in a day as to how much plum brandy we drank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the consumption of alcohol interfere with your performance of your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April of 1993 did the pace of your work as a liaison officer accelerate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did, enormously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that cause you to refuse some of the local's hospitality when it was offered to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about the beginning of April, 1993, I decided I would no longer drink plum brandy in the meetings, I would make an excuse about taking antibiotics or some other excuse so I didn't feel so tired every day from drinking so much the previous day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, did you start refusing the plum brandy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked whether you told investigators from the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor that your memory of events in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not very good. Let me ask you: Were you interviewed by an investigator from the Office the Tribunal Prosecutor named Mr. Montooth on the 19th of February, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page four of his interview notes, which were provided to the Defence by the Office of the Prosecutor, beginning of the first full paragraph, he wrote, and I quote, "DW," referring to Dundas-Whatley, "Has a good deal of information, and although he repeatedly suggested he had a bad memory, he soon recalled specific detail when specifics were discussed." End quote. Was that true? Did you recall specific details in this interview, although you apologised for not remembering more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This same interviewer from the Office of the Prosecutor, in February of 1995, wrote in the third sentence of the same paragraph, referring to you, and I quote, "He is more than willing to provide as much information as he can." End quote. Was that true? Did you cooperate with the Office of Tribunal Prosecutor in this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This same investigator also wrote three lines down in the same paragraph, on page 4 of his interview notes, and I quote, and this is a reference to you, "His loyalty to the British Battalion is without question, and particularly to his close liaison officer colleagues." End quote. How do you view your eight years of service in the British army, and what is your relationship with your former Cheshire Regiment colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was then and am now very proud of my regiment, and proud of the work that I did with them, both in Northern Ireland and in Bosnia. I was very proud, and still am, of my work and the work of my regiment in Bosnia of United Nations, and I was proud to serve the United Nations. My relationship now is as it was five or six years ago, with nearly all the officers in my regiment, I have a very close relationship with many of the officers who are still serving and many of the officers who are retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the last line of the interview notes of this Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor investigator, written of his interview with you on the 19th of February, 1993, reads as follows." If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you say '93?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, misspoke, you're absolutely right, Your Honour, 19th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I quote from the last sentence, and this is a reference to you: "If at all possible he," referring to Mr. Dundas-Whatley, "Should be interviewed before any statements are taken from the Cheshire Regiment officers." End of quote. Do you know why the investigator would say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only imagine that the investigators at last had found somebody who actually knew quite a lot about what had gone on in middle Bosnia and was very willing to cooperate; but more than that, I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said during cross-examination that you met the prior witness, Slavko Marin, at the airport in Amsterdam; could you explain how that meeting occurred and whether you had met him previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firstly, I had not met Slavko Marin previously, to my recollection. The meeting came about by what must only be a coincidence that I was at the Amsterdam airport, coming here to be a witness, and I met Counsel Anto Nobilo, who was had there to meet me, and with him, Slavko Marin was with him, as well, and that's how I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Nobilo for the purposes of transportation to The Hague to testify before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said on cross-examination that you were interviewed once by the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor on a particular occasion in the city of Split, Croatia. Where do you currently reside, in what city or town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live in the city of Banja Luka, which is in the Serb half of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also on cross-examination you were asked about the presentation of HVO bases in Central Bosnia; what did you mean when you referred or used that term, a base, a military base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the context that I answered the question, during the process of this trial, I was referring to places where we would see HVO soldiers, places where we knew they would be sleeping, like there would be quite a lot in a house or in a converted shop which they had taken over. Or it could be, I mentioned the Hotel Orient in Travnik and the Hotel Vitez, anywhere where a number of HVO soldiers would be stationed, in the school of Dubravica, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about HVO training in Central Bosnia. Did the HVO, to your knowledge, have a training facility in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown certain exhibits related to training, for the record, Prosecutor's Exhibits 484 and 456/104 through 108, and you said you were not surprised to see those documents, including certain orders for training issued by Colonel Blaskic. Can you elaborate as to why you weren't surprised to be shown those documents by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two things: Firstly, I was not surprised that Colonel Blaskic was making an attempt to train his soldiers. Secondly, I was not surprised, because all but one of those were dated before September, '92 when the situation between the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia was much more stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also shown certain combat orders, for the record, Exhibits D300 and P456/45 and 46. You were asked if you could deduce that they had been sent in a secure manner, that is via a secure communications method, and you said it would have been stupid not to send them via a secure communications method. Do you know how those orders in fact were sent by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be surprised based on what you learned about both the BH army and the HVO during your service if those orders were sent by an amateur software system that was, in fact, frequently intercepted by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not be surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked whether Colonel Blaskic, to your knowledge, asked the BH army to join in a joint investigation of Ahmici. Did UNPROFOR serve, on a regular basis, in the role of facilitating communications between the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Primarily through the use of our armoured vehicles. We frequently -- in fact, towards the end, we constantly moved HVO and Bosnian army commanders and negotiators around middle Bosnia to each others headquarters, or to pick them up and bring them to our headquarters for meetings and visits to the ground, constantly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why wouldn't, after the 16th of April, General Hadzihasanovic just come to the Hotel Vitez to visit Colonel Blaskic on his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For exactly the same reason. I can only guess, but I should imagine it's for exactly the same reason that Colonel Blaskic could not go to Zenica and visit the headquarters of the Third Corps. That is, they were at war with each other. It would be too dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were read certain passages from a magazine interview with then Colonel Blaskic, and from the testimony of a Prince of Wales' Own officer recounting his recollection of a discussion with then Colonel Blaskic. Those texts pertain, in part, to events in Ahmici in 1993, April of 1993. Can you tell us, with respect to information about ongoing criminal investigations within an army, is information concerning such ongoing matters in any army likely to be considered confidential and restricted information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly what security classification that type of information would go under, but it would certainly be information that would be closely guarded until a decision was made to publish the results of the investigation, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'd like to turn to the last topic, command and control in the HVO. You were shown, on cross-examination, a dozen or more documents consisting both of orders and reports. Earlier this morning I provided you with the following additional documents, Defence Exhibits 340, 341, 343, 213, 211, 148, 361, 363, 368, 75, 135 and exhibit -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 421, and I asked you to review those. Have you had a chance to review those exhibits prior to the commencement of this afternoon's court session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, taking into account your personal experience in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war, the documents that the Prosecutor asked you to review on cross-examination and the documents that you reviewed during your direct testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You want to leave a little time for the Office of the Prosecutor to have a quick look at those documents. Mr. Harmon -- can you identify them, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you for your consideration. Yes. If I have a problem, I will just interrupt briefly until I can get the appropriate document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Excuse me, Mr. Hayman. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Taking into account your personal experiences during your service in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as the documents you have seen subsequent to that service, both what you were shown by the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor on cross-examination, and the eight or ten documents that I asked you to review this morning, can you tell the Court, based on all of that information available to you, whether having that additional information, does it change or cause you to modify the opinions that you expressed to this Court both on direct and on cross-examination concerning the degree of command and control that existed in the HVO during your period of time serving with UNPROFOR in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The further documents that I've reviewed this morning only go to further reinforce my view that command and control was poor, and I have broken these documents down into three separate piles. The first pile are three documents that relate to the Ahmici situation, and particularly, the Ahmici investigation, and these are documents D340, 341 and 343. If I could briefly read you a little bit from 340. This document was written on April the 23rd --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go slowly. The interpreters don't have the documents in front of them. If you would like to read and place it on the ELMO that's fine, but in any event, please go slowly so that they can a full and fair opportunity to interpret. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document was written by Colonel Blaskic on April the 23rd. It's a letter written from his headquarters in Vitez to Colonel Bob Stewart, my commanding officer. And he says, "I am ready to send immediately the investigating commission to the village of Ahmici, as well as to all other places that need to be investigated because of gathering facts about all the innocent victims of this conflict. I myself beg you to help us stop this suffering and make the adequate conditions for the commission to work properly." There's some more paragraphs. In the final paragraph he says, "I consider to you be an utterly honourable and professional soldier." Then there are two other letters, in fact, two other orders, both of which were written by Colonel Blaskic, one on the 10th of May, '93 and one on the 17th of August, '93. The one from the 10th of May, and it's difficult to know exactly who it was sent to from the heading, but it comes out in the text, and it's titled, "Inquiry and Written Report on the Events in the Village of Ahmici", and then there's some background. "For several days various rumours have been circulating in the public regarding the events in the village of Ahmici since the 14th of May, '93." Now, I think he probably means the 14th of April because this letter was actually written on the 10th of April, but he says, "14th of May, '93, and the civilian casualties there." He then goes on and orders two orders. Firstly, "Gather all the information and submit a report on the events that actually took place in the village of Ahmici. In particular, on the number of casualties." The second part of the order, "I designate the assistance of SIS of the OZ in Central Bosnia as the person responsible for this task. The deadline is the 25th of May, '93." Before I come to the third document, what these two mean to me is that firstly, on or about the 23rd of April, Colonel Blaskic isn't fully aware of everything that happened in Ahmici, and he appears to be having trouble investigating it. So he's asking us to help him -- to help him. In other words, to provide security and possibly personnel to go to the village of Ahmici to begin an investigation, because he's hearing what he refers to two weeks later as rumours. But in the second one I read there, he's here giving an order to the SIS to go ahead and make an investigation of what -- and he says of what actually took place. The third document was dated the 17th of August, and again it's written by Colonel Blaskic, and this is again written to the SIS. I say it's again; this one is written to the SIS, and we know the last one must have been, because he's ordering them in the text of it. Now, this one is for three months later, just over three months later, and the order is, "In order to provide all the facts and take steps in further investigation in connection with killing the civilians in the village of Ahmici, the order, Point 1, to go on with making data and collecting information, considering the harm to civilians in the village of Ahmici." And further down he says, "The deadline for fulfilling this order is the 17th of September, '93." What this one means to me is that over three months since he last sent an order to this SIS unit, he doesn't appear -- although we don't know what went on between him and the SIS, he doesn't appear to have had the reports that he wanted. He doesn't appear to receive the information he's wanted. That is a clear indication that the command and control, and indeed communications between him and his subordinate units, if indeed the SIS were a subordinate unit, is not working properly. The second group of documents are a collection of orders and reports that were either written by Colonel Blaskic or received by him, and there is a further -- the first one, it appears not to have been written by him or received by him. The first one is Defence Exhibit 213. It's a very long document, and it was written on the 1st of March, 1993, long before the events in Ahmici. I won't read any of it, but I'll just summarise what it says. It's a very long document. It's a report written by the Military Police in Vitez and sent to the Military Police headquarters in Mostar. There is nothing on the document to suggest that it was also sent to Colonel Blaskic, but it may have been. It's all about an incident that took place in Vitez and Busovaca, I believe, but particularly in Vitez, in relation to the Military Police unit that was based there, took into custody, and then interrogated and got a lot of information from an individual who had been involved in criminal acts, and this report is written by that police battalion that was doing that investigation into these criminal acts, and the report lists a number of people who were -- as a result of that interrogation and other information, they found were also involved in various criminal acts, and some of these criminal acts appear to be quite violent. As the report goes on, it turns out that whilst in the Military Police custody in Vitez, this particular person was forcibly removed from the Military Police custody by a criminal gang that appears to have been led by some military policemen and others out of Travnik and other places. It's not necessarily an indication that the Colonel -- Colonel Blaskic's chain of command was particularly bad, it's an indication that the Military Police were not functioning properly and certainly were not functioning in the manner which a Military Police organisation must function if military discipline is to work properly, because whilst in Military Police custody, guarded by armed military policemen in uniform, presumably, this prisoner was released by other armed uniformed men, some of whom were also in the Military Police. The other documents from this second batch, all these were either sent by, or to, Colonel Blaskic. They're all Defence Exhibits 211, 148, 361, 363 and 368. The first one, written by Colonel Blaskic, he's referring to the destructive conduct of individuals in HVO uniforms, and he orders that persons inclined toward destructive and criminal conduct -- and he goes on about what should be done about them, and he gives a deadline of the 29th March. This document is written on the 17th of March. The next one, written --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just slow down slightly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The first one, on the 17th of March, went to a very wide circulation of commanders, HVO brigades, independent units, Military Police in Travnik and Vitez, HVO presidents and various departments. The second one, written on the 22nd of April, again to a very wide circulation, 12 brigades and various other organisations including the Military Police, the orders that he most strictly -- I quote, "I most strictly forbid the torching of houses and business premises and the looting of property." That's on the 22nd of April. Two days later, on the 24th of April, Colonel Blaskic sends another order to all the units in his zone -- in his Operative Zone, and it's titled, "Elimination of Arbitrary Acts by Commanders and Individuals -- by Commanders and Individuals", in the order. "After an assessment carried out in the field, it is apparent that the lower commanders and the units are acting outside the chain of command. They are not executing orders from superiors and are independently making decisions contrary to the received orders. They plan and execute their own combat activities, exert pressure on civilians and disrupt the work of UNPROFOR, ICRC and ECMM." Then he goes on to order, amongst other things, that all the organised troops are to be fully controlled and the commanders are personally responsible for the behaviour of the subordinates. He also orders that the individuals and groups who are completely out of control are to be arrested immediately and warrants are to be delivered to the command of the Military Police unit. He writes another order, also on the same day, to a very large distribution including the brigade in Busovaca, the brigade in Kiseljak, to the police in Vitez, "The unlawful --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, would you kindly identify the document you're referring to by number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise. This is Defence Exhibit 363, and the next one is 368. And he orders, and I quote, "Unlawful taking of the flats and stealing of property from the flats which belong to citizens, who for different reasons are temporarily not present, is to be prevented by all means" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please speak more slowly, Mr. Dundas-Whatley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try not to speed up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. "Unlawful taking of flats and stealing of property from flats which belong to citizens, who for different reasons are temporarily not present, is to be prevented by all means, including by use of force." And the final, dated the 31st of May, written by Colonel Blaskic, and it's sent to the 4th Military Police Battalion in Vitez and SIS. And I quote, "On the 30th of May, 1993, the officer on duty of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone informed me that these two people," who I won't say their names unless you particularly want me to, "Both members of the Military Police were expelling Muslim families by force. This was despite the order which bans such actions." It goes on to say, "In order to prevent further actions that hinder the execution of orders and the correct behaviour of Military Police," he goes on to order that they should conduct -- that the 4th Military Police battalion and the SIS should conduct an investigation, take disciplinary measures and send him a report by the 5th of June. Those five documents together, when you consider command and control within Colonel Blaskic's Operative Zone, those indicate to me that he is -- he is becoming aware that things are going wrong. He's becoming aware that illegal acts are being -- happening all over the place. But what it more indicates to me is that he is constantly, over a period of about six or eight weeks there, he's constantly having to send more or less the same order again to more or less the same people, stop burning houses, stop expelling people, and there's sending an order to the Military Police to tell military policemen to stop expelling Muslims from their houses. I think things were going quite badly at this stage for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that, can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if the military policemen are taking part in the illegal activities, expelling people from their houses, then who is going to stop it from happening?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last documents that I asked you to review, can you tell the Court whether they affect or cause you to change the opinions that you've given the Tribunal concerning the level or degree of command and control within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No at all. They simply reinforce the opinions which I stated last week and continue to hold at the moment. The first document is the Prosecution document number 421. This document was produced by the ECMM -- the ECMM office in Travnik on the 4th of July. It's a very long document and I'll summarise it. It's in relation to an aid convoy belonging to MSF Holland, Medicines Sans Frontier from Holland. There were four vehicles, it appears, and with four drivers. Three of them were French and one was English. They were all in possession of legal UNHCR ID cards. It appears from this report that this convey, consisting of medicines and other aid, arrived in Busovaca where it was stopped by the HVO, and the HVO arrested the drivers -- well, took the trucks and the drivers to a location and then arrested the drivers. Sometime after, the HVO Military Police arrived and told the HVO normal soldiers to go away and that the Military Police would handle the situation. Then sometime after that, the ECMM and some other international organisations got involved in the negotiations about these trucks, the humanitarian aid and the drivers. Very quickly the drivers were allowed -- were released, were allowed to be treated reasonably normally, and negotiations began in relation to moving of the humanitarian aid on, I think to Zenica, and I think some was going to Tuzla. And I quote, "The team suggested to transport the most urgently needed goods to their destination," and then there's a gap. "The legal and very urgently needed goods, medical equipment and medicines for Tuzla, and the powdered milk for Zenica would stay on the trucks and should be transported to their destination immediately." That was the suggestion of the meeting. The chief of the police, he's referring to the Military Police here, had to ask permission from his superiors in Mostar first. Had to ask his permission -- had to ask permission from his superiors in Mostar first. That document suggests to me that the Military Police chain of command came from Mostar, not from Colonel Blaskic. That's the indication that I draw from that. And now the final two documents. These both concern Colonel Alistair Duncan. Colonel Duncan commanded the BRITBAT after Colonel Bob Stewart. The first one an excerpt from a statement that Colonel Alistair Duncan made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, would you kindly identify the document by number? There should be an exhibit number on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Defence document 75 followed by Defence document 135. In this document 75, Colonel Alastair is talking about a convoy, the Convoy of Joy, which was interrupted by the HVO, and he's talking about his negotiations with regards to getting that convoy moved on. It's not unlike the story that I related to you last week. I'll only read two and a bit lines, two-thirds of the way down the big paragraph on this page 4899999. I quote, "The soldiers refused to allow the convoy to move, even when I used the name of Colonel Blaskic as an authority." It goes on, "The soldiers said quite categorically they wanted the order to come from" -- I won't say the name in court, but it was another senior figure in middle Bosnia at the time. And the final document, Your Honours -- I'm sorry this is taking quite a long time -- is Defence Exhibit 135, which is a -- it's a report of a meeting, written by Colonel Alistair Duncan, in August, '93. I'm reading from paragraph three. I'll miss out some names. He's referring to a Mafia Godfather, and it says in this report, "It would appear that this Mafia Godfather has considerable influence with the people of the Lasva Valley, whereas Blaskic does not, as proved by the events of the Convoy of Joy, where Blaskic proved to be nothing more than a puppet commander, ignored by the locals." Those last three documents, particularly the last, the one from the ECMM, I already told you that suggests that the military police were not responding to the Vitez chain of command but to the Mostar chain of command, and these last two from Colonel Alistair Duncan indicate strongly that Blaskic did not have a great deal of power in the Lasva Valley in relation to the Convoy of Joy, and these other people whose names appear in the documents had a great deal more authority than he had. His command and control was poor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. I have one other question for you of substance, but first let me ask you, what's on your lapel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is, we call this a poppy, and it dates back to the 1st World War when the British army was, the British army, and indeed the armies of the Commonwealth and the French army were fighting in France and Belgium against the Germans, and millions of people were killed, and they were killed in the fields of Flanders and elsewhere in Northern France, and at the time there were a lot of poppies in the fields. Ever since the armistice of the 11th of November, 1918, the British soldiers, and indeed Commonwealth soldiers, wear these every year to commemorate that war and every war that has followed subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have one more question for you, and that is, I would like to ask you whether you can confirm a particular incident or event which is recounted in your commanding officer's book "Broken Lives," Robert Stewart's book, "Broken Lives" and the incident described appears at the bottom of page 91 and carries over to the top of page 92. I will read you Colonel Stewart's description of the incident, and I would like you to tell the Court if you can confirm it, if you're familiar with it, and to what degree. "In Bosnia most forces fighting on all sides are from the local area. It is really a domestic war in many more ways than it at first appears. Suddenly a very large column of dispirited Croat soldiers, mostly in old cars and on tractor driven trailers, appeared in Vitez. They really did look a miserable sight. They all were perfectly willing to say what was happening, which was a clear indication to us that morale was very low. In fact, they just wanted to go home and were going to stay together until they did so. They were not soldiers at all, very few had had any real training. They could handle their weapons all right, but were really civilians in uniform. I asked them what they were paid, and they laughed. They were paid practically nothing, and certainly had no money at all for several weeks. In a normal army what they were doing would properly be called mutiny, but no army in Bosnia was normal. For two days, this large column stayed around Hotel Vitez, although once it tried to head west and then south to Gornji Vakuf, but was turned back by its own side. It was clearly very embarrassing for Tihomir Blaskic, the Croat commander of Central Bosnia. When I asked him about it, he simply shrugged his shoulders in a gesture of resignation. Eventually Blaskic agreed that the soldiers could go home, but they had to hand over their weapons in Kiseljak as they did so." Are you able to confirm this event and provide any greater context for the Court concerning it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can certainly confirm that it took place. The fall of Jajce was traumatic, and there was a massive influx of refugees, a lot of soldiers, a lot of civilians; but I don't think I can any add any more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the description in "Broken Lives" of a very large column of HVO soldiers from Jajce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That concludes my redirect examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you, I suppose you have some documents to submit as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: All the documents referred to are already in evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would move into evidence the exhibit that we tendered, 539.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see there is no objection. Before the Judges ask their questions, we're going to take a short 10-minute break, perhaps 15 minutes, and then, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, you will be asked some questions by the Judges and that will be all you will be asked to do. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we are ready to resume. Mr. Dundas-Whatley, after the direct examination, the cross-examination and the re-examination, I believe that the three of us Judges would like certain points clarified. Let me give the floor right now to my colleague, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Captain Dundas-Whatley, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can we continue calling you captain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not traditional below the rank of major to maintain one's rank after one leaves the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are living in Banja Luka now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am at the moment, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How long have you been there, and what are you doing, may I ask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been there on and off a long time, but I moved there permanently about a month ago, and I'm running a small business from that city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have a few points which I would like to understand more clearly, and I'm sure you will help me with it. You insisted on the fact that, of local loyalties, that the HVO was more or less a local army, and the loyalty was to the village or city, political leaders, if I understood rightly. Did that mean that any of -- not General Blaskic at that time, Colonel Blaskic's orders, combat orders; were they disobeyed, or the local authorities obeyed all the combat orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand the question. What I was describing was the -- I don't think it was just the HVO, I think it was -- what I was describing was also very true for the Bosnian army, was that the structure of the organisation was built locally, that, if you could compare it, for example, with the British army, which for more than a hundred years the British army has been used to decamping and going to other countries as battalions, regiment, divisions, brigades to fight wars. So, it was perfectly normal within the British military structure to have a chain of command and a fully functioning chain of command and a rank structure which could be transferred anywhere. People could be posted in and out of various headquarters, regiments could be attached to one headquarters or another. It's a system which has been in place for a long time, and it works very well. We do not have, in the British system, a problem with posting people or posting regiments under command of different divisions and different brigades. We don't have a problem where people say "I don't want to leave my home," or "I don't really want to go there and fight that war." I don't want to -- a British soldier or officer would not say "I don't think that's the job you want to do." But we have seen examples in the last few days, a very good example was in Fojnica, where the HVO military commander in Fojnica was given an order by Colonel Blaskic, as he was then, and then wrote back saying that he has consulted the priest and the various other organisations within the town and they don't really want to carry out the order. In fact, they refused to carry out the order. The reason was, as explained in that letter that I'm referring to from last week, was that the loyalty of the people in the town of Fojnica, the Croats in the town and the church and the other institutions which I can't remember right now, including the mayor, I think, and the other political representatives, was not, wherever the loyalty was, it was not to the HVO military chain of command. The HVO commander felt more loyal to the other civilian representatives in his town than he did to the orders he was receiving in a normal military chain, and that is a very good example of what I was talking to you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As you mentioned, and as we have been informed before, there was a chain of command since 1992, a chain of brigade, brigade commanders, we have been informed since the beginning, almost, of the trial; and you are confirming there was a chain of command of brigade commanders that existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did exist, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But, of course, there was this, as you said, religious influence. But do you have other very -- you mentioned before that example of the checkpoint when, I think it was you, you were passing, and they had to call Colonel Blaskic to take his opinion. You mentioned that was one of the examples of disobedience; but, in fact, they obeyed the order of General Blaskic, because you passed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They -- it was -- yes, I understand what you mean. I think not -- it wasn't that, in that particular case, that they obeyed the order of Colonel Blaskic. I think in that case they just realised that I was serious, that I was going to destroy that checkpoint if they did not let the convoy go through, even though they got an order from Colonel Blaskic over the phone. They swore at him and then slammed the phone down and then continued to be very angry, and I think it was the show of force outside, which was so often the case in Bosnia, the show of force and the real intent to use it, is what won the day on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned, also, something about the Muslim cleansing in Prozor when you arrived in October, 1992. Do you know how this cleansing took place? Could you just explain to us what you meant by this cleansing? Did they put them in buses to send them away, or did they, what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. Most of ethnic cleansing, most of the ethnic cleansing we witnessed in Bosnia was not in the style that you're talking about, the buses and so on. It was done through a process of fear and intimidation, that -- and this was on all three sides, all three sides -- but in the case of Prozor, it was the Croats taking control of the town, and all the Muslims then left because of some violence that was directed against them. There was some burning of shops and some burning of houses, and I presume, but I can't swear, that there was some shooting of Muslims in the town as well. But the result of the burning of the houses was the Muslim population felt very insecure in the town and so they left. They were terrorised, victimised and terrorised on ethnic grounds, so they left Prozor and the Croats had complete control of that town. Now, that style of ethnic cleansing was commonplace throughout the whole of middle Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who did the cleansing? Did you inquire, did you know who did the cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we knew it was the Croats, Your Honour, but as to which units and so on, I have no idea at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said the Croats; was it the police, was it the HVO? I mean, who had the weapons to do it? You said there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the military police, the civilian police, or the army, the HVO army, the normal army, or whether it was criminal groups. In the situation in Prozor, we were not first-hand witnesses of the initial phases of the cleansing. When I observed Prozor burning at the end of October, '92, what we saw was houses on fire, and the edges of the town were undergoing mortar fire, mortars were landing in villages around the town, and on the edges of the town, some, not a huge number. But it was enough to terrorise the population, the Muslim half of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I want to see something more clearly about Ahmici. To your knowledge, was the attack on Ahmici an organised one? Was it militarily organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to answer that. I presume you have heard first-hand accounts of people in the villages at the time, and I certainly have, and I presume you have some idea of the scale of the village. So, I don't think that it could possibly have happened unless it was planned, and to plan it and organise it, it had to have taken place. To answer your question, simply; yes, it must have been planned and organised, because it couldn't have been done by two or three people, it had to be done by a larger body of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And according to a systematic way, in a systematic way, not haphazardly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, we weren't there, we weren't aware until a week or so later. What I will say is I think most of the house burning, what I think -- this is a very personal opinion now, from many years experience, but without first-hand knowledge of what happened there, because I wasn't there. But from talking to many of the victims, myself, in the course of talking to friends and so on, I think there were two separate phases to it. I think there was the military side, which resulted in these horrible deaths, the 96 or so, hundred possibly, people killed, mainly women and children. I think the military side probably only took a few hours, maybe one day, and it was during that war, during that military attack, of some nature, that terrorising military attack, which must have been very fearful, it was during that phase that the population left. I think that the second phase was probably the looting and burning phase, and the destruction of the mosques, blowing up the mosques, burning the houses, a sort of scorched earth policy, which we are fully aware of in wars in that region, and throughout the world, anyway. I think that was over the day that is followed. So, I think it was two separate things. The first phase, the first part of it probably only lasted a few hours, but that's when the terror happened, and that's when, I think, all the death happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The terror happened by the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I say -- I don't know if it was military policemen or normal soldiers or bandits or criminals or what, I personally don't know which part of the Croat community committed that atrocity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, although there were these atrocities that existed, you mentioned that in an interview to this newspaper called Zagreb Danas Journal, Colonel Blaskic accused the Muslims of coming in to do this work, or even the Serbs, and even referred to Colonel Stewart as trying to spread false rumours, or even almost conniving with the Muslims. Now, at the same time you said that, or perhaps we concluded that, Colonel Blaskic ordered an investigation. Was this interview a result of the investigation? Did the investigation lead to the fact that Muslims themselves did that to themselves? Or was it a comment to influence the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I very much doubt if it was actually either of those, Your Honour. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: If there was an investigation, it would be asking the question, did they investigate to find out that this man did that thing. There is no need for an investigation in that case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You're right, but I don't think that that was the reason why Colonel Blaskic made the statement that he said. I must say I never saw the newspaper before Friday or Thursday, whenever it was, but I can only guess that -- I think that newspaper was October, '93, it was towards the end of the year, and I think probably by then the situation for Vitez and the Vitez pocket, the enclave, if you like, the Croats territory, surrounded as they were, that Colonel Blaskic found himself in at that period, I think the situation was probably very bad for the Croats. And I think possibly that newspaper article, he was using it for propaganda reasons. That would be my guess, that he was using it for propaganda reasons, to -- I mean, it would not, bearing in mind he was trapped in an enclave, it would not have been wise for him to, despite what he probably felt in his heart about the events of Ahmici, to go public and say that, well, we know it was committed by members of the HVO or members of whichever Croat organisation it was. It probably wasn't wise for him to do that. He would probably be more sensible not to speak about Ahmici at all until the investigation was complete. But he was concerned, I think, from reading the article, from the part that was translated, with the morale of his own army, which he -- and he knew it was an ill disciplined army, anyway, from these reports we spoke about. I think he was concerned with saying something which was likely to turn his army against him or against each other, when in fact their main concern at that stage was to continue to fight against the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But don't you think that would make the investigation pointless, if you are making an investigation and your boss decided the result beforehand. What is the need of the investigation? That is my inquiry. Because you already decided what the result was, what was the result was. And what was the reason for his reproach to Colonel Stewart in saying that he spread false rumours and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there any kind of animosity between him and Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not -- I don't think there was when my regiment left in the middle of May, '93, but there is one incident which comes to mind that may throw some light on some animosity that may have existed, and that was when Colonel Stewart went into Ahmici. I wasn't with him, but when he discovered, he was there when some of the, one of the younger officers and some other people discovered the horrific events there. He had television cameras with him, and he, he was recorded saying the words "bloody HVO", swearing at the HVO, in relation, I think, to the atrocity that had been committed. Subsequently that quote, whether it was in context or not, I have no idea, subsequently that quote was broadcast over one of the satellite channels, whether CNN or SKY, I don't know, and many Croats in Vitez and elsewhere saw this. So, I think it was enough people understood enough of the language to know what "bloody HVO" meant. So that moment of anger that Colonel Bob Stewart displayed, I think, was then thrown back in the faces of the Croats by the satellite broadcasters. I think that's what we're talking about here, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it on a special occasion, was it -- do you remember Ahmici, or what? Was it as a consequence of a massacre, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, I believe, and I wasn't there when he said this, I believe it was when he visited Ahmici for the first time, for the first time after the massacre; but I'm not absolutely certain about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned also that, lately, perhaps today, that several orders by Colonel Blaskic were given asking for an investigation and for disciplinary measures. It was, I think, addressed to the 4th Military Police Battalion, SIS, and these orders were not executed. There was no -- was there any follow-up, first, if you know about it? And if there wasn't, did he, did the matter, was the matter raised to the higher authorities, to explain or to notify that nothing has been done? Or was it just, was the matter closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was commenting on some documents that I saw, which were translations of orders that Colonel Blaskic had written. As to what the results of those documents, his orders were, I'm not entirely certain at all. Although, last week I was shown, on Thursday or Friday, I was shown a report written by the 4th Military Police Battalion on about the 16th or 17th, I think on the afternoon of the 16th of April, '93, where they, they went into no detail at all about what had happened in Ahmici, but said that, I think, Muslim forces from Ahmici had engaged -- it was a very minor description of what can only be described as a major event. And it appears that the 4th Military Police Battalion was stationed very close to Ahmici at the time. So, to answer that part of your question, did that happen as a result of the orders he wrote? Of course we never knew. I didn't see these orders until I came here to Holland. But it appears, the fact that he had to continually send the same order, continually write the same order so many times over a period of so many months, that he can't have been getting the results that, in the British army, we would expect as a result of the first order. We're not in the habit of having to repeat ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you don't know if it was raised to the higher authorities in form of complaint or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No document of that nature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Or asking if he had the authority to do it, the higher authorities, was there a higher authority to do it, which he can defer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the documents I've seen here, I think the higher military authority to Colonel Blaskic was probably General Petkovic in Mostar. That's how I understand it, but I'm afraid I'm going beyond my scope of knowledge here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But he was not in the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware Your Honour. I haven't been shown these documents. It would be wrong for me to draw any conclusions about that because I haven't seen any documents relating to that, apart from that one report shown to me on Thursday which made no mention of anything like that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You went also -- you explained to us that sometimes the raising of flags had an inflammatory effect, and especially when Mate Boban came, I think there was some trouble because they raised the Croatian flag. Was Bosnia, at that time, an independent State or not yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Legally and recognised by the United Nations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was no-man's land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Bosnia was an independent sovereign State from the previous year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They had a flag.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did have a flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And this flag was not the Bosnian flag which was being raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The point, Your Honour, is that by the time of the period we're talking about, Bosnia was divided not just into two, it was divided into three, and the Serbs -- the Serbs point-blank rejected the Bosnia flag, the Bosnia government and all the rest of it, and they controlled 70 per cent of Bosnia using Serb symbols, Yugoslavia Slav symbols, Serb symbols and the Cyrillic alphabet, et cetera, et cetera. In the other 30 per cent of the territory, which is what we're discussing, and Vitez and Travnik were in the other 30 per cent, there was a division there between the ruling government in Sarajevo, which we called the Bosnian government, which had the Bosnian flag, and they then ended up controlling something like -- I can't remember -- something like 15 or 20 per cent of the territory, something in that order. Although they were the established government, they only had about 15 or 20 per cent of the territory. And that's where their flag flew. Then there was the Croat territory which flew the Croat flag, and they had about -- a similar amount of the territory as well. So it wasn't that the Croats had just rejected the Bosnian government and the Bosnian flag, so had the Serbs. It was a three-way thing. And so the Bosnian flag was actually only flown in three major cities, which was Sarajevo, Zenica and Tuzla, and other towns like Travnik. But at the time we're talking about, Your Honour, if I could be absolutely clear, the Croat flag and the Bosnian flag were both in Travnik from the day I arrived and from before, because the HVO, which had the Croat flag, and the Bosnian army, which had the Bosnian flag, worked together in Travnik and Vitez and other towns, Gornji Vakuf, Zenica, many other towns, they worked together, so you could drive through the town and see both flags. The incident that you spoke about with regards to Mate Boban, we didn't see Mate Boban in the town. We were told that he had been there, and we were told that the presence of Mate Boban had inflamed things, because allegedly he -- whether he was there or not, I don't know, but we believed at the time that he was. That his presence inflamed things because he said, "Look, this is a Croat canton under the Vance-Owen Plan, and, therefore, the Croats' flag should be everywhere because this is a Croat canton under the plan," and that is what allegedly sparked the flag burning and shooting incidents of that day in the first week of April, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, I pass on another thing which you mentioned this morning about your -- I think somebody mentioned that you were ready to provide all the information you had to the Prosecutor, and, in fact, you were interviewed by the Prosecutor in Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've been interviewed many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you mentioned before, I think it was February 1995, one of them --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you said before that you refused once to sign a declaration. They wanted to you sign a declaration and you refused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've never signed a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When you're interviewed, don't you usually sign a declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my experience, and I have a lot of experience with this, the Prosecutor -- the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutors have visited me many times to clarify certain points. Now, over time, they have become much more knowledgeable about who was involved and what was happening, but as time has gone -- and as I speak to them, and I've spoken to them in Sarajevo, I've spoken to them in Zenica, I spoke to them in Split, I've spoken to them in many places, they, of course, like good investigators they write everything down. But on occasions they've wanted witnesses or potential witnesses like me to -- instead of them just writing down everything I say, they want me to make a statement to the Court, and I've never wanted to make a statement until I had much more knowledge about the subject matter, and until I was confident that the statement I was going to sign was accurate and correct and a full statement, and, furthermore, that I was willing to be a witness to that statement in -- and a witness to the Court as a result of that. Consequently, I have never signed any statements for anyone, because I think that all the -- all the cases in this Tribunal must be seen on their own merit and individually. And in the case of Colonel Blaskic, I have views which I've expressed in the last few days which I wanted to come here -- eventually I made a decision to come here and present those views in person to the Court. This would not have been helped by making a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean, you are not almost allowed to put your views in this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a different issue, Your Honour. There was an occasion where I was asked to sign a statement which was a statement that I hadn't written, almost as if I was incapable of writing my own statement, and I said, "I'd rather not."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. Just a rather personal question; you yourself said that you were -- when the Prosecutor was questioning you, you mentioned sometimes that you were often drunk, which I don't at all -- I fully understand that if anybody was living in these circumstances, it was better to be drunk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was not the reason why I was drunk. I was not searching for the bottle to make up for some other inadequacy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Turn away from the horrible views, perhaps, what you are seeing. But was it the case with all the people of the army? Were they trying to run away from the atrocities by getting drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was most definitely not the case, Your Honour, and it was not the case for me either. This -- this -- the point of the -- the point about the alcohol, I tried to explain it this morning, but I will -- this afternoon, but I will try again. There were six captains who were liaison officers, and I was one of them, and our job, our only job, was to talk to the local commanders. The battalion and the British in Bosnia at the time had something like 1,500 people and a whole regiment of engineers, I think, and lots of logistics people as well, but there were six of us, out of all these 1,500 people who had to spend all day every day talking to military commanders and civilian leaders. Most members of my battalion and most members of the British army didn't meet locals. They saw them occasionally at checkpoints, they didn't meet them. Many members of the battalion didn't go outside the British base the whole time they were in Bosnia, because their job didn't require them to. Then there were people on patrol like the companies, like Major Thomas' company, Colonel Thomas as he is now, who went out on patrols, and to observe the front-lines and observe other things, and they were in and out whole time and they would see the locals. But there were six of us who were out the whole time with the locals, and the custom we found was that -- and I think possibly we encouraged it as well, but the custom we found is that when we went into somebody's office, we would be given a cup of coffee and a glass of brandy. And the coffee always tasted horrible and the brandy always tasted horrible, but if you alternated it would become a little bit nicer. And we got -- and this would happen every day. So if I had ten meetings in a day, I would probably be quite drunk at the end of it. But I knew this was happening, and so I wrote everything down in my notebook so I didn't have to rely on my memory, and when things got really busy I made a decision that I would stop drinking. I was not the only one. I made a decision that I would refuse their hospitality, which was okay because they knew me by then. They all knew me very well, so refusing the hospitality did not matter in the sense of upsetting the commanders. Does that answer your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does. Now, the last question: Concerning the 7th Muslim Brigade, you mentioned that they were different from the people in the area, and that even some Bosnian officers complained to you about them and mentioned that they were fundamentalists. That was your word, I think. In other words, they were religious fanatics. Would you then conclude that the other Bosnians, the Muslim Bosnians were not Muslim fanatics? Is that a fair conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, Your Honour. The overwhelming percentage of Muslims and Croats and Serbs, but Muslims, to answer your question, are not fundamentalists in their religious or other beliefs. They are perfectly normal, sensible people. That's what was so particularly worrying about the formation of the 7th Muslim Brigade, because it wasn't what anyone expected in Bosnia. Bosnia does not have a history of Islamic fundamentalism. In reality, I think many of the people who joined the 7th Muslim Brigade themselves were not fundamentalists at all, but it was a better army to join -- not a better army, but a better part of the army to join, because they were paid more, they were given uniforms, and in the event of them dying, their families would be cared for properly, which -- there were other advantages for them to be with the 7th Muslim Brigade, but there was an unity of purpose within the 7th Muslim Brigade. It was very attractive for the Muslims. And it attracted those, of course, who had more deep religious views and were capable and wanting to fight as well. But that was what was so worrying about it, is that most Muslims in Bosnia, and I have many Muslim friends in Bosnia, of course, are perfectly rational people who do not posses religious or other fundamental views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So there was no religious barrier between Muslims and non-Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not prior to this war. The problems that nationalism create are they -- as we've seen in Northern Ireland and all over the world, nationalism unites people behind one cause or one flag at the expense of all others. So the Muslims and the Croats separated, and they ended up being united behind their own flags at the expense of each other. Instead of uniting behind one flag, as they have subsequently managed to do with the Federation, which is progressing quite well in Bosnia right now. But back in '93, religious -- sorry, nationalism, not fundamentalism -- nationalism was a very powerful force. It was in the hands of very irresponsible, power crazy, many of them young people. It was stirred up by criminal groups who benefited from the anarchy and chaos which it brought about, and it allowed criminal gangs to loot and pillage. If you create Croat nationalism in a Muslim area, the Muslims leave and you go and take the car and the television. So I think there are a whole load of reasons why nationalism was very successful in middle Bosnia, and part of it was this religious fundamentalism, this religious divide that you're talking about, but that wasn't the historic cause of it in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, anyone who has listened to you, as we have these last days, would be puzzled to know how anyone could possibly have the temerity to expect that you would sign a statement which did not represent your full and true views. Where were you when this statement was written up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't sign the statement, and I was -- this took place in Sarajevo last -- last year, Your Honour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, but where were you when this statement was being written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, in my flat in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement was being written in your flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
