utterances.text: No, I was -- I -- an investigator came to my flat and asked me if I would sign the statement and was it suitable for me to sign, and of course, I said "No." He, I believe, had written the statement as a result of a conversation we'd had the previous day or the previous week in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, he had written it up before coming to your flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And did you read it or did he read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I remember, he showed it to me and I said, "I have no intention of signing a statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How many pages was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say several pages or one page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't remember, Your Honour, because the whole idea of being asked to sign a statement written by someone else was -- seemed ridiculous to me, and I said this to the investigator at the time, and he was quite happy with this. I must point out he was quite happy with this. I think he realised he asked me please -- would not -- please sign, but he said, "Could you sign this," or, "Would you sign this statement it would be quite good for us if you-- or quite useful if you would sign a statement, words to that effect." I can't remember the exact words. And I said, "No." So I can't actually remember -- I think the statement was brought out, put on the desk. I don't think we even turned it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. So would I be correct, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, in concluding that you refused to sign the statement on the basis of the principle that any such statement should have been written by you? Is that a way of looking at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's partly it, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It was not a question of the statement containing any specific inaccuracies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour, and if that's been the suggestion, then I'm very sorry. That was never meant to be the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I was interested in your career having been demobilised. Is that the right word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It used to be Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Demobilised from the army because it was slimming down. You then served with certain NGOs, I think Oxfam was named, and you lived for a while in Belgrade and later on in Sarajevo, and later on in Banja Luka, or were there other places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've also lived -- when I was with Feed the Children, I lived in Vitez, Your Honour, which is particularly relevant, and I have lived in Split in Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good. And you operate a business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could I ask what business is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I act as a consultant for people. For example, I do a lot of work -- not so much now, but historically I did a lot of work for the press, for the international press. More latterly, in the last year or so, I have -- I provide a lot of services, facilities, for the International Community, in particular the -- for example, I -- it would be inappropriate for me to mention some of my clients, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please feel completely secure, and do not trouble to mention any clients about whom there might be the slightest sensitivity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there's no sensitivity, I just think that -- for example, I manage a house for the British Embassy. I don't do it personally, but we -- the British Embassy have contracted me as a consultant to organise a house for them and manage it for them on the coast. We do -- I would do that type of thing for other organisations, which I don't need to list, I don't think. We -- our big drive in the last two years has been towards leisure for the International Community, and we do a great deal of skiing for the British army. We hosted all the British army skiing in Bosnia last winter, including -- we run their ski meetings towards the end for the British division. And we do sailing for the international organisations, where we act as a broker between the international organisations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What is the scope of your contribution to the international media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is coming to an end now, Your Honour, because of course, the international press are not too interested in the events in Bosnia so much now, but normally I -- they -- I'm -- I've got a title such as "coordinator," something like that, and I provide interpreters, and I would probably drive the news crew around, or documentary company. I must point out that I was involved in the documentary on The Hague last year, although I didn't actually come here, I did the Bosnia end of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would I be right in supposing that your contribution to the international press would be concerned mostly with the events about which you speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you wouldn't be, Your Honour. It's -- the documentary was partly concerned with Vitez, and it was -- but no, most news is not interested in this. I didn't start working for news until the summer of '95, autumn '95, by which time the events of Ahmici were long forgotten as a news item. No, it's things like the election or the opening of the bridges in Mostar or -- the elections are a very big and ongoing story, every time there's an election or appointing of governments. Sometimes the introduction of the single currency, the new single currency in Bosnia. Events like this that take place in the course of time attract the international media, and they need someone on the ground to organise things for them, to organise camera crews for them and vehicles, and know what's going on and to have the contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good. Then would I be right in supposing that in the course of your contribution to the international press, you would have had occasion to speak on the subject of command and control in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. I don't remember discussing command and control with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other British officers like you who settled down in the former Yugoslavia after leaving the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's one from my regiment which I'm aware of, Your Honour, who lives in Sarajevo, and there are quite a few British people working there as well. I wouldn't say we've settled -- any of us have settled down there, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you have a family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You don't have a family. You're a loner. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just not married to my family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Once or twice, perhaps more often, in the course of your testimony, you assured the Court that you were not being evasive. Why did you feel it necessary to give that assurance? I don't believe --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember a specific example, but I think -- I think occasionally I would be asked a question which required a more complicated and in-depth answer than a simple yes or no, or a number, or date, and so in order to explain it, I would have to come in from a slightly different angle, and that's what I was referring to, things that happened in Bosnia and continue to happen in Bosnia are not necessarily as simple as people may wish to believe them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Am I right in my recollection that neither Defence counsel nor prosecuting counsel used the word "evasive"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us talk about Prozor a little, through which you passed in October 1992. The prosecuting counsel was asking you a question like this: Did tensions rise as a result of the ethnic cleansing in Prozor? My recollection is that your answer was that tensions rose because of the influx of refugees in certain places. Now, which is it really? Did the ethnic cleansing by itself in Prozor cause tensions to rise, or did tensions rise solely because of the subsequent influx of refugees into certain places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's going to be a long answer, Your Honour. In most of the towns and most of the cities in Bosnia, the HVO and the Bosnian army worked together, but then -- as the relationship between the two of them started to collapse, from the south heading northwards, what happened in one town may have almost no effect on a town 50 miles way, or that we could see. So were it not for the fact that Prozor had this horrific situation which resulted in a loss of confidence on the front lines in Jajce, which resulted in refugees coming into Vitez, which were explained in the book just now, it is unlikely that the results of Prozor would have had a direct effect on Vitez, because the Vitez situation, like the situation in all the towns further north, was a power struggle and a balance. But the refugees came, a lot of Muslim refugees came from Banja Luka, Jajce fell and that caused a strain, and that reverberated down the Lasva Valley, from Travnik down to Vitez and further. But at the same time -- we're talking now about October, '92 -- at the same time in Tuzla, a 100 miles or so away, the HVO and the Bosnian army co-operated throughout the war and this had no effect on them. And so it was -- and at the same time, Vitez and -- in Vitez, the Muslims and Croats in October, '92, were shooting each other in the streets, but in Travnik they're walking down the streets together, only 20 miles away. So what I was trying to answer -- what I was trying to explain in that answer, is that, yes, Prozor was ethnically cleansed, but one of the main results of that as the collapse of Jajce, and the influx of refugees, and the loss of confidence between the two sides locally, and to some extent regionally, but it did not cause panic and despondency further down -- further down the chain. The HVO in Sarajevo and Tuzla were -- continued to co-operate perfectly with the Bosnian army. Do you understand why I wanted to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me square my understanding with yours. Your position is that the ethnic cleansing in Prozor did not, by itself, cause tensions to rise in places further afield; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. I understand your answer. Now, are you in a position to say to the Court, in a ballpark sort of way, whether you considered that a substantial part of HVO personnel had come to the HVO with or without previous JNA experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the overwhelming percentage of the population in Bosnia had JNA experience, but, I also believe, and this is, of course, hearsay, that at some stage the, many people in Bosnia started not attending their compulsory military service. They didn't bother to go, the system was collapsing, I think probably in '90 or '91. So, yes, there were young people of military age that did not have military experience, but it was, of course, a minority when put against the overwhelming majority who had served in the JNA 20 years before, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that, therefore, to follow the drift of your remarks, that the HVO did not have greater JNA experience than the ABiH? Is that what you would say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have thought -- this is not an area I'm an expert in, none of us were, none of us are -- but I would have thought that the percentages would be very similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very similar. Thank you. What about equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The, from what we saw, and from what we knew from talking to people who had been on the Serb side, the Serbs had overwhelming military might, in the sense of equipment, tanks, artillery, so on. Left on the other side, on our side, if you like, where we were stationed, there wasn't actually a great deal of military hardware around, and to see an artillery piece going down the street was a major event. So, I don't think that -- and the most number of tanks I ever saw in one day was two, and they were probably 30 miles apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask your impression on this point about which the Court has had the benefit of other testimony. How would you compare the fire power exerted from the Vitez side against the fire power exerted from the Stari Vitez side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in taking that isolated area together --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Over a sustained period of time, say during the whole of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't ever see any heavy weapons in Stari Vitez. I saw rifles, I didn't -- I don't remember ever seeing mortars, tanks, artillery in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What I mean, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, is; was the level of fire power the same, or was it preponderant in one side or preponderant on another side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably I saw very little hardware. I think probably the Croats had, in that, in the Vitez town, had more heavy equipment than the Bosnian army. But we're not talking about tanks here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about fire power, whatever the source be, rifle, tanks, mortars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. Well, I think it is then down to how many people that the Croats could put on that front-line, because the Croats had another front-line as well, the outside front-line looking out towards Zenica and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What I mean, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, was; there was an armed exchange between Vitez and Stari Vitez which went on for a while. Now, which side had the preponderance of fire power, or did they have roughly the same level of fire power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I should imagine the Croats outnumbered them, but I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did the HVO control the territory through which the resupply routes of the ABiH passed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Generally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely right, Your Honour, yes. Except that there were stories that, there were stories, and I never confirmed it, that in Travnik the Bosnian army was actually getting resupply also from the Serbs, but I think it is more of a black market nature than anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us turn to HV, the wearing of HV insignia, that is, the military emblems of the army of Croatia proper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: My recollection is that you said you saw only one insignia being held up by some instrument or another, a pin or something. Were you aware, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, that the then Colonel Blaskic had issued instructions to his military to order them to discontinue the wearing of any HV emblems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Assuming that he did so, would that make a difference to your evidence that you did not see any soldiers in HV uniforms or wearing HV insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I can only remember one occasion where I saw an HV insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us talk a little about another subject. Did you become aware of some degree of cooperation between the HV and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HV and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The HVO, I'm sorry, the HVO and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but this was after I left the army that I was appraised of all this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Never mind when you became aware of it, you did become aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: There was a degree of cooperation between the HVO and the army of the Republika Srpska. Could you tell us a little more about the nature of that cooperation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The, there are a few examples that spring to mind, Your Honour. For example, in the area of Kiseljak we were aware, or I became aware, as an aid worker travelling through Kiseljak, that as you went from Croat territory to Serb territory, there were no bullet holes in the walls, which was normally the best indication of front-line. So, it appeared to us, then, that Kiseljak, although it had a front-line with the Serbs, and indeed with the Bosnian army, as well, it was not in a shooting war with the Serbs, indeed, there was traffic crossing that front-line. So there is that incident of cooperation that I was aware of in '94. Also in '94 I became aware of what had gone on in the town of Zepce, which I mentioned to you before, it's well to the north of Zenica. Zepce was, in my time, had an HVO and a Bosnian army headquarters in the town. Subsequently there was a small war in the town and the Bosnian army was kicked out and the HVO took control of the town. During -- that came about, I've been told, because of cooperation between the HVO commander in that town and the Serbs who came across the front-line and assisted the HVO in their war against the Bosnian army in the town of Zepce. So, those are two examples that spring to mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you become aware at any stage of a covering umbrella agreement between Serbia and Croatia under which this, these incidents of cooperation might have occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember reading something in the newspaper, some, probably in '94 or '95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you read anything about talks being held at -- what's that name, Karadjordjevo, between President Milosevic and President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The press spoke about this frequently, that, it's not something that I'm aware of at all, Your Honour, but the press spoke about this frequently, that there was a master plan. Whether it involved Mr. Izetbegovic or not, I'm not sure, but there was, allegedly, a master plan to divide Bosnia up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan came along and it assigned Canton 10 inter alia to the Croatian community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe Travnik was Canton 10, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could you help the Court by telling us how the HVO understood the assignment of Canton 10 to the Croatians? Did they understand it to mean that the HVO were to control it, or did they also understand it to mean that Canton 10 was to be cleansed of any non-Croatian elements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it was the latter, but I think what happened was, when the Vance-Owen Plan was produced and divided Bosnia into all these cantons, it was, part of the plan was that each canton would be ruled by one of the three parties, and that is how we understood it. We were having trouble getting enough information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you could help us by telling us how the HVO understood it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how we understood it, and I believe that Mate Boban's alleged visit to Travnik was him saying that Travnik is the capital of Canton 10, this should be under the control of the Croats, why aren't the Croat flags everywhere. I think that's the way the Croats saw it. But in, the real situation was, the Croats knew in Travnik, in the town of Travnik, that they were hopelessly outnumbered in terms of numbers of soldiers, but also in the fire power that was available to the Bosnian army in Travnik, because of the huge number of refugees which had come in from Republika Srpska, that it was better, that Colonel Filipovic probably thought it better to leave things as they were, rather than trying to impose some sort of control over Canton 10. But I think what you described is how the Croats thought it was meant to be but were not in a position to do it. I do remember attending a meeting on this issue in Travnik, and the HDZ representative, that's the Croat political party representative, for the town of Travnik, was a man whose name was Krizanac, his nickname was Klempo because he had sticking out ears, and that's how I remember him, he was a very odd looking man. And his politics were slightly less balanced than people like Colonel Filipovic. He was, I believe he was from Travnik, and I think he went to school with the, with my interpreter's aunt. He was a great one for screaming and shouting and banging the table, and he did this at this meeting, and it got so annoying for everyone at the meeting that the military part of the meeting, which was Colonel Alagic and Colonel Filipovic and their staff officers and aides, and me and my interpreter, we decided to adjourn the meeting and have another meeting which would have no civilians at it, because it was the HDZ representative in Travnik that was causing all the problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What was he saying on this point of Canton 10 being or not being exclusively occupied by Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he would have been, he would have been strung up there and then if he said anything like that in that meeting. That may have been his personal views, I don't know. But he was, um, if I remember, and I haven't got any notes about it, because it was such a ridiculous conversation I didn't write anything down, but as I remember it, he was complaining to the Croat military leaders that they were weak and should take control of the town. And this was in front of the Bosnian army commanders, as well. It was a ridiculous situation to be in. The military commanders like Colonel Blaskic had much more understanding of the real situation on the ground, and they weren't about to start inciting in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: They had a saner assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: They had a saner assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Tell me, was there any question, did you ever become aware of Herceg-Bosna giving an ultimatum to the BiH to this effect that if the BiH, Mr. Alija did not sign on to the Vance-Owen Plan, the Croatian community would unilaterally implement the plan? Did you become aware of any such ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. But I do remember something about that, but it was much later that I, and probably in '94 or '95, when I was reading a book by a journalist that I remember something about that. It was not an issue during my time in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If it had arisen during your time in the army, would you have considered it sufficiently important to engage your attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, an ultimatum of that nature, Your Honour, would have -- ultimatums by their very nature have a destabilising effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What you read in the books was about an ultimatum to implement the Vance-Owen Plan effective the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember a date being involved. I don't remember there being a date. What I do remember, and this is well out of my scope of knowledge, Your Honour, but, well out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I only ask you because you were there, and you said you had been visiting a number of the officers on both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan was a constant topic of conversation through March and April, '93, right up to the events this Court is concerned with, primarily. I think that the opinion that many journalists hold on this, and it is not an unrealistic opinion, was that the Vance-Owen Plan, the very presence of, whether it was signed or not, or an ultimatum or not, the very presence of it is what resulted in the Muslim-Croat war in Bosnia, the complete collapse, the rush for land, the grab for land. I don't remember reading that, the ultimatum that you're referring to, that I think was in a book by Vulliamy, I believe, who may have testified in this case, I'm not sure, referred to a date, I think -- I do remember something in probably his book about this, about there being some sort of ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, speak once or twice about the Vance-Owen Plan, or perhaps I'm mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this Court, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I referred to it on one occasion, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let's turn to a separate subject which relates to command and control. The thesis you presented was that based on your experience on the ground, and looking at the documentation, command and control was flimsy, I think you used the word, and it best sums up the totality of your testimony on the point; is that what you were saying, that it was flimsy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that in some documents Colonel Blaskic reminded his soldiers that International Law relating to armed conflicts applied -- I'm paraphrasing a great deal of documentation here. You're aware that he took that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware that he ever used that phrase, Your Honour. It's not been in any documents I read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think he referred to the Geneva Conventions and International Law and to the International Humanitarian Law. If I'm wrong counsel on both sides may correct me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He may have used the word Geneva Convention, but I'm not entirely certain, Your Honour, but he certainly spoke about the points of those laws, if not mentioned them by name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you are a military man, yourself, and you are familiar, I take it, with the rough outlines of that area of law as it applies to military men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, we all know it covers several branches, but is it your impression that a central idea in that law relates to the question of command and control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the sense that a commander is responsible for the actions of his subordinates, to some extent; is that what you're referring to, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do I gather from what you are saying that as you see it, nobody, just nobody had any command and control responsibility for whatever happened in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, far from it, Your Honour, I most definitely am not saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, could you tell us what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I am saying is in the -- in the specific case of Ahmici, for example, a very good example, an attack happened on that village resulting in a lot of people being killed, and that attack must have been controlled by somebody, or a group of people, and it must have -- so under their control there must have been a larger number of people. So, it was a planned and organised attack, I'm sure, although, I didn't witness it, of course, I believe it was a planned and organised attack, but probably on a much, much lower level than the OPS group level or even the brigade level. I think it is far more likely that it was -- talking about that one for a moment -- that that attack was planned and orchestrated at a lower level, you could probably say at company level, if you were to compare it with a British army, something of that nature. Furthermore, the -- we used to refer to -- I still do -- refer to the state of middle Bosnia and the Lasva Valley, at the time in question, as being in anarchy. But by that we didn't mean that everyone was out with a gun doing what he wanted. What we meant was there was gangs, criminal gangs, small military, quasi military units, that the central power and the chain of command did not follow what we had written down on the big wall of our MILINFOSUM, with Petkovic at the top and OPS group, Central Bosnia and Tomislavgrad I think was the other one, Mostar, I'm not sure, and the various OPS groups, and underneath them the various brigades, and under them whatever the battalions were, I can't remember. That was a chain of command, and it looked good on the wall, and any visiting generals would see that and think we had a good idea of what was going on; but we would then tell them that actually there were many other influences and that -- so, I'm sorry, but if I could finish -- that there was a chain of command on paper, and there were a lot of things that were happening in the town, and they weren't random. But that does not mean that they were as a result of the main, the military chain of command that we understood. We knew there were criminal gangs, we knew Bob Stewart had to personally negotiate for the release of vehicles that had been hijacked or stolen, so did Captain Martin Fulgrave, who was a liaison officer in the Lasva Valley prior to me, he had to personally negotiate with people. But the people we were negotiating with were not the brigade commanders and Colonel Blaskic. It was other people, it was some political figures on occasion, some criminal figures on occasion. Does that answer your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley, it's always interesting and rewarding to listen to you. I'll ask you my last question. I gather, from what you are saying, understandably, that a number of variables have to be taken into account in evaluating any situation. Now, would there be a distinction, do you think, between certain kinds of orders? On the one hand you have combat orders which are telling troops to attack or to retreat or to encircle the enemy or something like that. I would call those combat orders, but I would defer to your more accurate description. On the other side you have other kinds of orders, say orders relating to safe passage of convoys, or non-torching of houses, or non-expulsion of people; do you see what I mean? There is a distinction, I would suppose, but only suppose, between combat orders and other kinds of orders. Now, is it within your knowledge that any combat orders issued by Colonel Blaskic were disobeyed with impunity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the information I have relating to anything like this I have learned much more recently, from a documentary point of view, from the documents, orders that I've seen in court, for example. I think the example of Fojnica, where the brigade was given an order to link up, to protect the southern flank of the pocket, I think that summarises the order, this area down here, which was point blankly refused. So, there is that example which has come to my notice in the last four days. But if I could go back to the question: In the British army we don't draw distinctions between these different types of orders, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, I know, the British army is a very superior kind of military model. I was offering you a distinction and inviting you to say whether you would make that distinction. Are there other incidents like Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any other incidents at the moment, Your Honour, I haven't seen enough documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did Fojnica concern, and I really don't know, did Fojnica concern the question of obedience to a combat order to engage the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I probably would have to study the order in more detail, Your Honour. But the impression it creates and that its response creates, to me, is that the brigade there was asked to take military action in one or two villages, I can't remember, and refused to do that. The, all the impressions I have created are a result of everything, not a result of one particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I appreciate that, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, and I do thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think after the questions that my colleagues asked it won't be necessary for me to ask any. I want to thank you very much. I see that my colleague, Judge Riad, would like to ask you an additional question, apparently. All of them were asked, Mr. Riad, remember we have a break to take for the interpreters' sake. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Point of clarification, I was under the impression, when I asked you about your refusal to sign the statement with the investigator, I was under the impression that you were not in agreement with the substance of the statement; but in your answer to the searching question of my colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, you mentioned it was the result of an interview, and the whole thing was that you did not, you wanted it to be in your own style, that was the only reason. So, I want just a clear answer, was the statement the result of the interview, and it was just prepared for your convenience; or was it a statement of things you don't want to sign? That's the first. The second: If you didn't, if you are, being a journalist and a writer, you wanted to write it yourself; why didn't you do that, since you have been telling us several times that you are only in search of the truth and it was an occasion to tell the truth. Did they prevent you from writing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I didn't -- I don't remember whether I read the statement -- the statement they wanted to be signed or not. I don't think I read it. I think what happened, if I can remember -- this was only a minor point and I am very surprised it has become an issue, it is a minor point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not, Your Honour. For me it was not a big issue. The issue at the time was that I didn't want to -- there were two things, I didn't want to sign a statement which I hadn't written myself. But, secondly, I didn't want to sign any statements anyway, because at the time of the interview I didn't have the benefit of all these notebooks which I kept at the time. I knew my memory was -- I do not have a good memory, and I know that, so I was very concerned about putting my pen to paper on things which, even if I believed them to be absolutely true, which until I had been back to Britain, found my notebooks, which were dotted all over the place, and had the benefit to sit down and talk to people who knew a lot about the situation and be briefed fully, particularly, if possible, read the MILINFOSUMs and the other documents which my regiment produced, which there are an enormous pile of documents, then I would be in a better position to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the statement was a result of the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interview was the day before, but I presume so, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It is normal to make a statement after an interview, that is what I wanted to make sure of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would make a request of the Court, and that is, Mr. Dundas-Whatley has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we're going to first take a break. I really want to keep in mind the interpreters. You can take the floor once the break is over, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Dundas-Whatley leaves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dundas-Whatley will be back in the courtroom to hear your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I think that you had -- that you had requested be given the floor. I suppose it is a statement relating to that statement; is that correct? The statement in the Prosecutor's office. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we yield the floor. We have no additional information or requests to the Court, and we're prepared to proceed with the next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think then as regards the testimony, Mr. Dundas-Whatley, the Tribunal sends you back to your job, and thank you for having come.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps you might at least introduce the next witness in order to gain some time, Mr. Nobilo. I only have the English version in front of me which introduces the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I shall briefly present the next witness to you. The next witness is the father -- is Father Ivan Pervan, a clergyman. He belongs to the Franciscan Order, and he is the clergyman in Kiseljak. He will be explaining where he comes from, what schools he has completed, and he will say a few words on the importance of the Franciscan Order in Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout history. After that, he will describe his community and parish, the territory it encompasses. He will be speaking about his work as the leader of Caritas, the humanitarian organisation, which sent aid and assistance both to Croats, Serbs and the Muslims during the war. He will be speaking about the refugees which appeared in the municipality of Kiseljak, where they came from, who they were fleeing from, and the number of refugees that came and individuals dates when the refugees arrived, so as to be able to get an impression of what actually happened in Kiseljak. They will then be speaking about the village of Rotilj, and he went to the village of Rotilj personally and took food to the Muslim population there. He will describe the conditions under which the Muslims in Rotilj lived and what he remembers from that time. Furthermore, he will speak about how Kiseljak came by its food supplies, what the roads were and communications were via Serb territory that were used to take humanitarian aid to the needy. And Father Ivan was personally in charge of the convoys passing across Serb territory to Split, where in the port of Split food was taken over and that was the food that, in fact, fed the population of the Kiseljak municipality. He will indicate the directions used, the exact directions used, and how these directions were used for other commercial purposes and military purposes. He will also be speaking about the way Kiseljak was cut off as an enclave from Vitez and Busovaca, the second enclave, as he saw it from his own position, and he will be speaking about his meetings with Tihomir Blaskic, what they discussed, his assessment of Tihomir Blaskic as an individual, as a man, and he will be speaking about what he learned about relations between Tihomir Blaskic and Ivica Rajic, the commander of the brigade in Kiseljak, and Blaskic as commander of the Operative Zone, and from his aspect -- from his angle of vision, how he saw the functioning of the chain of command and control of the command. Then he will speak about Miel Borzic (phoen) who was at one time the commander of the Ban Josip Jelisic Brigade, and the circumstances under which he was expelled from the command of the Ban Josip Jelisic Brigade, and under what circumstances and conditions he was reappointed -- Ivica Rajic was reappointed as commander of the Ban Josip Jelisic Brigade. Well, that would be a summary and a praecipe, and the testimony could last up to three hours, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Three hours. Very well. We'll have the witness brought into the courtroom (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me? First of all, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, give us your name, your first name and what people generally call you, since your religious work was described to us briefly. First state your name, your first name, where you work, and what name you would like the Tribunal to use when speaking to you, and after that you will take the oath. For the time being remain standing, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Ivica Pervan. That is the name I was given at birth, Ivica Pervan. I am by vocation a clergyman, and everybody addresses me as Father Ivan Pervan. I am a clergyman in the Kiseljak parish. I have been since the 1st of September, 1991, up to the present day. I would like you to address me as Father Ivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you like. This is a question you would ask of the President of the tribunal, but it is self-evident that the Judges may have a different sensitivity. This is an International Tribunal, they will call you as I see fit, but I was asking what in general people call you. Obviously, our colleagues, according to their own sensitivities, will call you what they feel is appropriate. For the time being you are Mr. Ivica Pervan. Remain standing are for a few more moments, the time it takes to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may be seated. This is the end of the afternoon, but we still have about 15 minutes, which will allow Mr. Nobilo to begin with his direct-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good evening, Father Ivan. We shall try, in the 15 minutes at our disposal, to cover some basic information about you and the Franciscans, and we'll continue tomorrow with other concrete matters. Father Ivan, tell the Court, please, where and when you were born, what schools you have completed and where you have worked so far.

utterances.speaker: IVICA PERVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was born on the 16th of December, 1957, in the place of what Nadiocivitsa (phoen) of the Maglaj municipality, and I completed, in my native village, eight years of primary school. In 1973 I graduated and went to classical gymnasium in Visoko. I graduated four years of the classical gymnasium, and then I went to Sarajevo where I attended the Faculty of Theology. I also completed the Raijal (phoen) gymnasium in 1978 in Zagreb, and the Faculty of Theology I graduated in -- that is I went in Sarajevo, and graduated in Ljubljana Slovenia in 1983 as a clergyman, and as such I was sent to the Lepenica parish, which is 10 kilometres away from Kiseljak, which is where I spent one year. After that I went one and a half years in Travnik in the Rajkovici (phoen) parish, after which I spent three years as the vicar of -- in the monastery in Kresevo. After that I was assistant for three years of the clergyman in Busovaca, and I have been in Kiseljak for eight years. I am the parish priest there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the Franciscan Order? I think we should speak a little more slowly so the interpreters can follow us. Your order, the Franciscan Order, came to Bosnia in 1292. So tell us briefly -- tell the Court, briefly, under what circumstances the Franciscans came to Bosnia and what they mean to the history of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: IVICA PERVAN
utterances.text: Bosnian history has recorded that Bosnia gained its statehood, Your Honours, in the 11th Century, and that statehood is always mentioned, and the name of Kulinbahn (phoen) was mentioned, and it says that "There have never been better days than the days of Kulinbahn." So the 11th Century is the century I'm talking about, which is when the church had its hierarchical organisation, and the Bisjuanova (phoen) is mentioned as a place which is the Vitez of today, which was the headquarters of the bishop, and it had Bishopric and it had three churches. With the Bosnian Kingdom, especially with the Kotrominic (phoen) Dynasty, there were closer links formed as was usual and customary in the Europe of the day between the King and Rome. The King asked the Pope in Rome to send to Bosnia missionaries who would teach his people and who would spiritually educate and lead the people. The Pope replied by sending him the Franciscans, and at the time the King's seat was in Central Bosnia in Sutjiska (phoen) at the town of Bobovac, and in 1292, was the year when the Franciscan Order arrived in Bosnia. The Franciscans remained in Bosnia, remained in Bosnia to the present day, and they make up more than half the Bosnian Catholic clergymen. With the downfall of the Bosnian monarchy under the -- under Turkish rule in 464, the King was killed, the Queen fled to Rome, and the Franciscans have remained in Bosnia to the present day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: 464? Did I hear correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 1464. It's a mistake. 1464. There was a mistake in the translation of the name (sic). In 1464 was when Bosnia fell. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: IVICA PERVAN
utterances.text: To the present day, nobody in Bosnia and Herzegovina is contesting the fact that somebody does not -- that people do not have a 700 year old continuity except the Franciscans, and we celebrated the 700th anniversary of the Franciscans in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the meeting. At this celebration we had the presence of all the church dignitaries and the State dignitaries headed by the President, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Since the downfall of the Bosnian monarchy in 1464, the Franciscans remained the sole people to offer resistance -- to support the Catholics in Bosnia-Herzegovina right up until the arrival of the Austro-Hungarian Empire in 1878, and throughout that time they erected their settlements, which are called monasteries, and which on several occasion were set fire to by the Turks. New ones were built which incurred a lot of heavy material costs, and certificates for these to be built up from Istambul. They were the protagonists of education, they were the sole physicians, the sole builders in the country, and they were the first to write a grammar of the language of our people. They were also the sole representatives with the authorities of the time, and in this period of almost 500 years, nobody was able to have power and authority unless they were under the rule of the Turkish Empire and an Islamist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, is it true that when the 700th anniversary of the Franciscans arrival in Bosnia, is it true that the president of Bosnia, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, said that the Franciscan Orders are the oldest part of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, therefore, the fathers, Franciscan fathers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA PERVAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, and we were very happy to hear this. He told us that in a long speech that he made on the occasion, and he said this with pride. He said -- and we accepted this, and recognised it as recognition for all the good that we had done for the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now explain to the Court, and we shall be completing this now, your parish, what places does it incorporate, the parish of Kiseljak, and is there a difference between the parish of Kiseljak and the territory of the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVICA PERVAN
utterances.text: The Kiseljak parish is located in Central Bosnia, and it takes the name of the municipality of Kiseljak. It has the same name. It is the town proper, the town itself, but the municipality of Kiseljak incorporates three more parishes, the Banba Lepenica (phoen) to the south of the municipality, in the middle we have the Kiseljak parish, and then we have the Gromiljak parish. Next to it the Brestovska (phoen) parish. So we can say that is a central town urban parish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the town of Kiseljak, what other large place belongs to your parish?

utterances.speaker: IVICA PERVAN
utterances.text: To my parish belongs the town itself, and also the surrounding villages linking up on the town. The largest village which belongs to the parish of Kiseljak is quite certainly the Brnjaci community, Calukovac, Potkraj, Palez, Zagorice, Zavrsje, Veljko Selo, Podastinje, Parizevici, Rotilj, and one part is called Privori, then we have Borina, both the Borinas, Kresevska Cesta and Cizma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was the introductory part; so, before we go into the substance of our examination-in-chief, perhaps we could break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we will suspend the hearing. We resume tomorrow at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
